A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PhD research work, with readable main text, figures, tables and references. Neither contains an appendix, although v2 explicitly assigns generation prompts, evaluation templates, task-level results and CLIP-analysis details to an appendix. Those unavailable materials limit comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.6 and Tables 2–3 report original data-quality assessments and experimental evaluations of five LVLMs.

after.justification: Table 4 and Figure 3 report original model and benchmark evaluations. Section 4.2 also reports original CLIP similarity diagnostics.

M1.justification: V1 generates confusing items primarily through ChatGPT prompts over annotations. V2 introduces task-specific candidate vocabularies, CLIP image-text ranking and manual hitem correction, plus two-stage narrative-context generation. Its ChatGPT–Doubao pipeline also generates CCS images, replacing v1's manual collection approach. These substantially revise benchmark construction.

E1.justification: The five-task organization largely regroups existing tasks: sentiment, position and counting already appeared under attributes in v1. However, v2's stated benchmark excludes utility questions, absurd/unanswerable questions and real CCS images. Three tone-based statement checks give way to questions accompanied by inaccurate or incorrect narrative contexts, substantially changing the tested input conditions.

E2.justification: V2 retains the five original named models and adds LLaVA-1.1, LLaVA-1.6 and GPT-4o, alongside 13B variants of LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-1.6 and InstructBLIP. Table 4 therefore contains eleven configurations. Figure 3 also introduces AMBER as an empirically evaluated benchmark comparator alongside POPE.

E3.justification: V1 uses accuracy, open-ended answer matching and separate positive controls. V2 uses balanced paired binary questions, harmonic Yes/No-recall scores averaged across tasks and modes, and explicit image-priority instructions for context modes. It introduces size comparisons and the PhD-2k subset specifically for GPT-4o. Reported benchmark size changes from 53,976 questions to 102,564 triplets.

E4.justification: V1 examines absurd-question formats, statement tones and attribute differences. V2 substantially revises the context analyses and adds model-size comparisons, LLaVA evolution across benchmarks, and a CLIP diagnostic testing whether visual features distinguish CCS content from ordinary descriptions. These address additional robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: V1 Table 3 reports point estimates only; v2 Table 4 adds ± quantities to recall and F1 entries. The supplied text does not define these quantities or give repeated-run counts or seeds. The reporting addition is established, but repeated-run uncertainty estimation cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: The main performance results are extensively replaced. V1 Table 3 reports mPLUG-Owl2's highest average hallucination accuracy of 65.6%; v2 Table 4 ranks Qwen-VL highest among open models with a PhD score of 0.50 and reports GPT-4o at 0.77 on PhD-2k. Figure 3 adds POPE/AMBER evolution results. Changed datasets and metrics prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.6 introduces a mathematical score definition: its F1 is the harmonic mean of Yes-Recall and No-Recall, with further averaging across tasks and modes. This changes the defined evaluation quantity relative to v1's accuracy metric. No theorem or proof development appears in the available material.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contribution on four intrinsic hallucination types and an automated benchmark pipeline. V2 redefines the contribution around a task-by-mode framework with twenty combinations and scalable generation including CCS images. Its conclusion additionally emphasizes open models' weakness relative to GPT-4o under misleading textual contexts.

C2.justification: V2 develops v1's modality-imbalance account into three structural sources involving visual features, modality alignment and internal knowledge. Section 4.3 newly interprets why larger LLMs can help inaccurate-context understanding while harming some visual or CCS evaluations. It also connects model evolution to visual training and qualifies GPT-4o as a reference with undisclosed specifications.

D1.justification: V2 identifies GPT-4o mini instead of v1's GPT-3.5 and documents Doubao, vocabulary sources, counting range, correction/inpainting procedures and evaluation hardware comprising eight V100 GPUs on Linux. Conversely, generation and evaluation templates are deferred to the unavailable appendix, and v1's benchmark access link is absent. The available reproducibility documentation changes substantially.

R1.justification: V2 replaces much of v1's model and hallucination-mitigation survey with positioning by visual-task level and objective versus subjective evaluation. It adds works including NOPE, CIEM, MMMU and IllusionVQA, and centers comparison on objective recognition benchmarks. V1's discussion of methods such as OPERA, Woodpecker and Volcano is absent from the supplied revision.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, construction section and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Terminology changes from LVLM/IVL-Hallu and confusing items to MLLM/VHE and hitems. Construction is reorganized into pipeline stages, while per-type experimental sections become consolidated results and discussion sections.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 with an architecture schematic, combines and substantially revises the earlier examples and pipeline in Figure 2, and adds performance curves in Figure 3. Tables are rebuilt into a benchmark taxonomy, expanded data overview, CCS-generation examples and a model-by-mode performance display. These substantially change the visual organization.

improvement.justification: V2 improves response-bias controls through paired questions and balanced scoring, and adds useful model-size, evolution and CLIP diagnostics. However, its promised appendix and v1's access link are absent, ± statistics remain undefined, and correction rates do not establish final data quality as v1's sampled assessment attempted to do. Table 2 also leaves CCS task counts totaling 750 unreconciled with 1,500 Yes/No questions. These design benefits and unresolved validation and reproducibility gaps prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
